lesson_title: The Siren That Lies: the Doppler Effect
hook_text: The ambulance siren drops its note as it passes you. Except... it never changed. Your ears got played.
clip_script: An ambulance screams toward you — high, urgent note. It passes — and the note suddenly sags, deeper. Ask the paramedic inside: the siren held ONE steady note the whole way. So who changed it? You did, just by standing there. Sound is a parade of crests leaving the siren, evenly spaced. Driving toward you, every new crest launches from a bit closer — the parade arrives bunched up, more crests per second, higher pitch. Driving away, each crest starts from farther back — the parade stretches, fewer per second, lower pitch. The siren never lies; the spacing does. And that little street-corner trick runs serious machinery. Hospitals bounce ultrasound off flowing blood: the moving cells shift the echo's frequency, and the shift reads their speed — that's how a clinic finds a narrowed artery, and how parents hear a foetal heartbeat, no needles involved. Point the same idea at the sky and it gets bigger: light from almost every galaxy is shifted toward the red. Shifted red means moving away. Everything is leaving, and the farthest galaxies are leaving fastest. One sagging siren, one expanding universe — same physics, one equation.
visual_style: Wavefront circles bunching ahead of a moving ambulance and stretching behind it; cut to an ultrasound probe with a shifting echo trace and a heartbeat pulse; zoom out to galaxies with their spectral barcodes sliding redward.
mood: Street-level and then suddenly cosmic — one trick scaling three sizes.
pacing: Siren pass with an audible pitch sag, tight wavefront explainer, two-beat application montage, expansive close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and master the one equation that reads speed from sound and light.
